title: 04. AsyncIO: AsyncIO Synchronization
summary: Covers Why Async Synchronization?, asyncio.Lock, asyncio.Semaphore, asyncio.Event, asyncio.Condition and more.

sections.title: 10.1 Why Async Synchronization?
sections.body:
### Visual Explanation

```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║              SYNCHRONIZATION IN ASYNCIO                                     ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  "But wait, asyncio is single-threaded! Why do we need locks?"              ║
║                                                                             ║
║  THE PROBLEM:                                                               ║
║  ────────────                                                               ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Task 1:    read counter ─────► compute ─────► await ─────► write counter  ║
║                                                    │                        ║
║                                                    │ CONTEXT SWITCH!        ║
║                                                    ▼                        ║
║  Task 2:    ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ read counter ────► compute   ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Task 2 reads the OLD value before Task 1 writes the new value!            ║
║                                                                             ║
║  WITH LOCK:                                                                 ║
║  ──────────                                                                 ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Task 1:    ┌─── LOCK HELD ────────────────────────────┐                   ║
║             │ read ─────► compute ─────► await ─────► write │               ║
║             └──────────────────────────────────────────┘                   ║
║                                                              │              ║
║                                                              ▼              ║
║  Task 2:    ░░░░░░░░░░░░ [waiting] ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ read ─► compute   ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Task 2 waits for Task 1 to release the lock!                               ║
║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### When You Need Async Synchronization

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    WHEN TO USE ASYNC LOCKS                                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│  ✅ USE ASYNC LOCKS WHEN:                                                    │
│  • Read-modify-write with await in between                                   │
│  • Shared resource access across async operations                            │
│  • Rate limiting concurrent access to external APIs                          │
│  • Coordinating order of async operations                                    │
│                                                                              │
│  ❌ DON'T NEED LOCKS WHEN:                                                   │
│  • Pure computation without await                                            │
│  • Each task works on independent data                                       │
│  • No shared mutable state                                                   │
│                                                                              │
│  ⚠️ NEVER USE threading.Lock with asyncio!                                   │
│  • threading.Lock is blocking (freezes event loop)                           │
│  • Always use asyncio.Lock                                                   │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

diagrams.title: Races still happen in asyncio — at await points
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Task A
  participant S as balance = 100
  participant B as Task B
  A->>S: read balance → 100
  A->>A: await bank_api() — suspends
  B->>S: read balance → 100
  B->>S: write 100 − 80 = 20
  A->>S: write 100 − 80 = 20
  Note over S: two withdrawals of 80, balance is 20 instead of failing
diagrams.explain: asyncio is single-threaded, so code *between* awaits is atomic — but any `await` inside a read-modify-write lets another task interleave. Use `asyncio.Lock` (not `threading.Lock`, which would block the whole loop) around such sections.

sections.title: 10.2 asyncio.Lock
sections.body:
### Visual Explanation

```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                         ASYNCIO LOCK                                        ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║                    ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                     ║
║                    │           LOCK                   │                     ║
║                    │                                  │                     ║
║                    │     State: 🔒 LOCKED             │                     ║
║                    │     Owner: Task A                │                     ║
║                    │                                  │                     ║
║                    │     Waiting Queue:               │                     ║
║                    │     ┌─────────────────────┐     │                     ║
║                    │     │ Task B │ Task C │ ...│     │                     ║
║                    │     └─────────────────────┘     │                     ║
║                    │                                  │                     ║
║                    └─────────────────────────────────┘                     ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Methods:                                                                   ║
║  ────────                                                                   ║
║  • async with lock:     → Acquire and auto-release                         ║
║  • await lock.acquire() → Acquire lock                                     ║
║  • lock.release()       → Release lock                                     ║
║  • lock.locked()        → Check if locked                                  ║
║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Basic Lock Usage

```python
import asyncio

# Shared state
counter = 0

async def increment_without_lock():
    """Unsafe increment - race condition!"""
    global counter
    temp = counter
    await asyncio.sleep(0.001)  # Simulate async operation
    counter = temp + 1

async def increment_with_lock(lock):
    """Safe increment with lock"""
    global counter
    async with lock:
        temp = counter
        await asyncio.sleep(0.001)  # Simulate async operation
        counter = temp + 1

async def main():
    global counter

    # Without lock - race condition
    print("=== Without Lock ===")
    counter = 0
    tasks = [increment_without_lock() for _ in range(100)]
    await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    print(f"Expected: 100, Got: {counter}")  # Usually less than 100!

    # With lock - safe
    print("\n=== With Lock ===")
    counter = 0
    lock = asyncio.Lock()
    tasks = [increment_with_lock(lock) for _ in range(100)]
    await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    print(f"Expected: 100, Got: {counter}")  # Always 100!

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Example 2: Lock as Context Manager

```python
import asyncio

class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, balance=0):
        self.balance = balance
        self.lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def transfer(self, amount, target_account):
        """Transfer money to another account"""
        # Always acquire locks in consistent order to prevent deadlock
        first, second = sorted([self, target_account], key=id)

        async with first.lock:
            async with second.lock:
                if self.balance >= amount:
                    # Simulate network delay
                    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
                    self.balance -= amount
                    target_account.balance += amount
                    return True
                return False

    async def get_balance(self):
        async with self.lock:
            return self.balance

async def main():
    account1 = BankAccount(1000)
    account2 = BankAccount(500)

    print(f"Initial: Account1={await account1.get_balance()}, "
          f"Account2={await account2.get_balance()}")

    # Concurrent transfers
    tasks = [
        account1.transfer(100, account2),
        account1.transfer(100, account2),
        account2.transfer(50, account1),
    ]

    await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

    print(f"Final: Account1={await account1.get_balance()}, "
          f"Account2={await account2.get_balance()}")
    # Total should still be 1500

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

sections.title: 10.3 asyncio.Semaphore
sections.body:
### Visual Explanation

```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                         SEMAPHORE                                           ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  Semaphore = Lock that allows N concurrent holders                          ║
║                                                                             ║
║  asyncio.Semaphore(3):                                                      ║
║                                                                             ║
║  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  │    Slots: [✅] [✅] [✅] [❌] [❌]  (3 of 5 available)              │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  │    Active:     Task 1, Task 2                                       │   ║
║  │    Waiting:    Task 3, Task 4, Task 5                               │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   ║
║                                                                             ║
║  When Task 1 releases:                                                      ║
║                                                                             ║
║  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  │    Slots: [✅] [✅] [❌] [❌] [❌]  (Task 3 gets slot)              │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  │    Active:     Task 2, Task 3                                       │   ║
║  │    Waiting:    Task 4, Task 5                                       │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Use cases:                                                                 ║
║  • Rate limiting (max N concurrent API calls)                               ║
║  • Connection pooling (max N database connections)                          ║
║  • Resource throttling                                                      ║
║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Rate Limiting API Calls

```python
import asyncio
import time

async def fetch_url(url, semaphore):
    """Fetch URL with rate limiting"""
    async with semaphore:
        print(f"Fetching {url}...")
        # Simulate API call
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
        print(f"Got {url}")
        return f"data from {url}"

async def main():
    # Max 3 concurrent requests
    semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(3)

    urls = [f"http://api.example.com/item/{i}" for i in range(10)]

    start = time.time()

    tasks = [fetch_url(url, semaphore) for url in urls]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"\nFetched {len(results)} URLs in {elapsed:.2f}s")
    # With 10 URLs, 3 concurrent, 1s each: ~4 seconds

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Example 2: Connection Pool Pattern

```python
import asyncio
import random

class AsyncConnectionPool:
    def __init__(self, max_connections=5):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(max_connections)
        self.connection_count = 0

    async def get_connection(self):
        """Get a connection from the pool"""
        await self.semaphore.acquire()
        self.connection_count += 1
        connection_id = self.connection_count
        print(f"Connection {connection_id} acquired")
        return connection_id

    def release_connection(self, connection_id):
        """Release connection back to pool"""
        print(f"Connection {connection_id} released")
        self.semaphore.release()

    async def execute(self, query):
        """Execute query using pooled connection"""
        connection_id = await self.get_connection()
        try:
            # Simulate query execution
            await asyncio.sleep(random.uniform(0.1, 0.5))
            return f"Result of '{query}' on connection {connection_id}"
        finally:
            self.release_connection(connection_id)

async def main():
    pool = AsyncConnectionPool(max_connections=3)

    queries = [f"SELECT * FROM table{i}" for i in range(10)]

    tasks = [pool.execute(query) for query in queries]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

    print("\nResults:")
    for result in results:
        print(f"  {result}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Example 3: BoundedSemaphore

```python
import asyncio

async def demonstrate_bounded():
    """Show difference between Semaphore and BoundedSemaphore"""

    # Regular Semaphore - can release more than acquired
    regular = asyncio.Semaphore(2)

    await regular.acquire()
    regular.release()
    regular.release()  # No error, but now has 3 slots!
    regular.release()  # Now 4 slots!

    print(f"Regular semaphore: no error (but broken!)")

    # BoundedSemaphore - prevents over-release
    bounded = asyncio.BoundedSemaphore(2)

    await bounded.acquire()
    bounded.release()

    try:
        bounded.release()  # Error! Already at max
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"BoundedSemaphore: {e}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(demonstrate_bounded())
```

diagrams.title: Bounding concurrency with asyncio.Semaphore
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  urls["1 000 fetch coroutines"] --> sem{{"async with Semaphore(20)"}}
  sem -->|"20 in flight"| api["remote API"]
  sem -->|"980 waiting"| q["suspended, not blocking the loop"]
  api -->|"one finishes, releases"| sem
diagrams.explain: `gather` over 1 000 coroutines starts them **all at once**, which can exhaust sockets, connection pools or a partner's rate limit. Wrapping the request in `async with sem:` keeps at most N in flight while the rest wait cheaply.

sections.title: 10.4 asyncio.Event
sections.body:
### Visual Explanation

```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                           EVENT                                             ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  Event = Simple signaling mechanism                                         ║
║                                                                             ║
║  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   ║
║  │                           EVENT                                      │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  │                    State: ⚪ UNSET                                   │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  │    Waiters: [Task A] [Task B] [Task C]                              │   ║
║  │              (all blocked on event.wait())                          │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   ║
║                                                                             ║
║  After event.set():                                                         ║
║                                                                             ║
║  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   ║
║  │                           EVENT                                      │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  │                    State: 🟢 SET                                     │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  │    All waiters wake up immediately!                                  │   ║
║  │    [Task A ✓] [Task B ✓] [Task C ✓]                                 │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Methods:                                                                   ║
║  • event.set()        → Set the event (wake all waiters)                   ║
║  • event.clear()      → Clear the event                                    ║
║  • event.is_set()     → Check if set                                       ║
║  • await event.wait() → Wait until set                                     ║
║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Startup Coordination

```python
import asyncio

async def database_init(ready_event):
    """Initialize database"""
    print("[Database] Initializing...")
    await asyncio.sleep(2)  # Simulate slow init
    print("[Database] Ready!")
    ready_event.set()

async def worker(worker_id, ready_event):
    """Worker that waits for database"""
    print(f"[Worker {worker_id}] Waiting for database...")
    await ready_event.wait()
    print(f"[Worker {worker_id}] Starting work!")
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return f"Worker {worker_id} result"

async def main():
    ready_event = asyncio.Event()

    # Start workers and database init
    tasks = [
        asyncio.create_task(database_init(ready_event)),
        asyncio.create_task(worker(1, ready_event)),
        asyncio.create_task(worker(2, ready_event)),
        asyncio.create_task(worker(3, ready_event)),
    ]

    await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    print("All done!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Example 2: Pause/Resume Pattern

```python
import asyncio

class PausableWorker:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.pause_event = asyncio.Event()
        self.pause_event.set()  # Start in running state
        self.stop_event = asyncio.Event()

    async def run(self):
        """Main worker loop"""
        counter = 0
        while not self.stop_event.is_set():
            # Wait if paused
            await self.pause_event.wait()

            # Do work
            counter += 1
            print(f"[{self.name}] Working... ({counter})")

            await asyncio.sleep(0.5)

        print(f"[{self.name}] Stopped after {counter} iterations")

    def pause(self):
        self.pause_event.clear()
        print(f"[{self.name}] Paused")

    def resume(self):
        self.pause_event.set()
        print(f"[{self.name}] Resumed")

    def stop(self):
        self.stop_event.set()
        self.pause_event.set()  # Ensure not stuck on pause

async def main():
    worker = PausableWorker("Worker1")

    task = asyncio.create_task(worker.run())

    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    worker.pause()

    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    worker.resume()

    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    worker.stop()

    await task

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

diagrams.title: asyncio.Event for start-up and shutdown signals
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant W as Worker tasks
  participant E as asyncio.Event
  participant M as main
  W->>E: await ready.wait()
  M->>M: open DB pool, warm caches
  M->>E: ready.set()
  E-->>W: all waiting workers resume
diagrams.explain: Identical in spirit to `threading.Event`, but `wait()` is awaited so it suspends a task instead of blocking a thread. A shared `stop` event that every loop checks is a clean way to implement graceful shutdown.

sections.title: 10.5 asyncio.Condition
sections.body:
### Visual Explanation

```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                         CONDITION                                           ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  Condition = Lock + Event (wait for condition to be true)                   ║
║                                                                             ║
║  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  │   Producer:                                                          │   ║
║  │   ─────────                                                          │   ║
║  │   async with condition:          # Acquire lock                      │   ║
║  │       buffer.append(item)        # Modify shared state               │   ║
║  │       condition.notify()         # Wake ONE waiter                   │   ║
║  │                                  # Lock released on exit             │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  │   Consumer:                                                          │   ║
║  │   ─────────                                                          │   ║
║  │   async with condition:          # Acquire lock                      │   ║
║  │       while not buffer:          # Check condition                   │   ║
║  │           await condition.wait() # Release lock, wait, reacquire    │   ║
║  │       item = buffer.pop()        # Use shared state                  │   ║
║  │                                  # Lock released on exit             │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Methods:                                                                   ║
║  • await condition.wait()      → Release lock, wait for notify, reacquire  ║
║  • condition.notify(n=1)       → Wake up n waiting tasks                   ║
║  • condition.notify_all()      → Wake up all waiting tasks                 ║
║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Producer-Consumer with Condition

```python
import asyncio
import random

class AsyncBuffer:
    def __init__(self, max_size=5):
        self.buffer = []
        self.max_size = max_size
        self.condition = asyncio.Condition()

    async def put(self, item):
        """Add item to buffer"""
        async with self.condition:
            # Wait while buffer is full
            while len(self.buffer) >= self.max_size:
                print(f"[Producer] Buffer full, waiting...")
                await self.condition.wait()

            self.buffer.append(item)
            print(f"[Producer] Added {item}, buffer: {self.buffer}")

            # Notify consumers
            self.condition.notify()

    async def get(self):
        """Get item from buffer"""
        async with self.condition:
            # Wait while buffer is empty
            while not self.buffer:
                print(f"[Consumer] Buffer empty, waiting...")
                await self.condition.wait()

            item = self.buffer.pop(0)
            print(f"[Consumer] Got {item}, buffer: {self.buffer}")

            # Notify producers
            self.condition.notify()
            return item

async def producer(buffer, producer_id, count):
    for i in range(count):
        item = f"P{producer_id}-{i}"
        await buffer.put(item)
        await asyncio.sleep(random.uniform(0.1, 0.3))

async def consumer(buffer, consumer_id, count):
    for _ in range(count):
        item = await buffer.get()
        await asyncio.sleep(random.uniform(0.2, 0.5))

async def main():
    buffer = AsyncBuffer(max_size=3)

    await asyncio.gather(
        producer(buffer, 1, 5),
        producer(buffer, 2, 5),
        consumer(buffer, 1, 5),
        consumer(buffer, 2, 5),
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Example 2: Wait for Specific Condition

```python
import asyncio

async def wait_for_condition():
    """Demonstrate condition.wait_for()"""

    condition = asyncio.Condition()
    data = {'value': 0}

    async def waiter(threshold):
        async with condition:
            # Wait for specific condition
            await condition.wait_for(lambda: data['value'] >= threshold)
            print(f"Threshold {threshold} reached! Value: {data['value']}")

    async def updater():
        for i in range(1, 11):
            await asyncio.sleep(0.3)
            async with condition:
                data['value'] = i
                print(f"Updated value to {i}")
                condition.notify_all()

    await asyncio.gather(
        waiter(3),
        waiter(5),
        waiter(8),
        updater(),
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(wait_for_condition())
```

sections.title: 10.6 asyncio.Barrier
sections.body:
### Visual Explanation

```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                           BARRIER                                           ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  Barrier = Synchronization point for N tasks                                ║
║                                                                             ║
║  asyncio.Barrier(3):  # 3 tasks must reach barrier                          ║
║                                                                             ║
║  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  │    Task 1: ████████████──────────┬──────────► continues             │   ║
║  │                                  │                                   │   ║
║  │    Task 2: ████████──────────────┤ BARRIER                          │   ║
║  │                                  │ (all wait here)                   │   ║
║  │    Task 3: ██████████████────────┴──────────► continues             │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  │    When Task 3 arrives, all 3 are released!                         │   ║
║  │                                                                      │   ║
║  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Use cases:                                                                 ║
║  • Phased computation (all must complete phase before next)                 ║
║  • Game loops (all players ready before starting)                           ║
║  • Parallel initialization                                                  ║
║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### Code Example

```python
import asyncio
import random

async def worker(barrier, worker_id):
    """Worker that synchronizes at barriers"""

    # Phase 1: Initialization
    print(f"[Worker {worker_id}] Initializing...")
    await asyncio.sleep(random.uniform(0.5, 2))
    print(f"[Worker {worker_id}] Init complete, waiting at barrier...")

    await barrier.wait()
    print(f"[Worker {worker_id}] Phase 1 complete!")

    # Phase 2: Processing
    print(f"[Worker {worker_id}] Processing...")
    await asyncio.sleep(random.uniform(0.5, 1.5))
    print(f"[Worker {worker_id}] Processing complete, waiting...")

    await barrier.wait()
    print(f"[Worker {worker_id}] All phases complete!")

async def main():
    # Create barrier for 4 workers
    barrier = asyncio.Barrier(4)

    # Start workers
    tasks = [worker(barrier, i) for i in range(4)]
    await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

    print("\nAll workers finished all phases!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

### Visual Explanation

```
║                         ASYNC QUEUE                                         ║

║  Queue Types:                                                               ║
║  ────────────                                                               ║
║  • asyncio.Queue          → FIFO                                           ║

║  • asyncio.PriorityQueue  → Priority-based                                 ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Methods:                                                                   ║
║  • await queue.put(item)  → Add item (blocks if full)                      ║
║  • await queue.get()      → Get item (blocks if empty)                     ║
║  • queue.put_nowait(item) → Add without blocking (raises if full)          ║
║  • queue.get_nowait()     → Get without blocking (raises if empty)         ║
║  • queue.qsize()          → Current size                                   ║
║  • queue.empty()          → True if empty                                  ║
║  • queue.full()           → True if full                                   ║
║  • queue.task_done()      → Mark task as processed                         ║
║  • await queue.join()     → Wait until all tasks done                      ║
║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Worker Pool Pattern

```python
import asyncio
import random

async def producer(queue, count):
    """Produce items"""
    for i in range(count):
        item = f"item-{i}"
        await queue.put(item)
        print(f"[Producer] Added {item}")
        await asyncio.sleep(random.uniform(0.1, 0.3))

    print("[Producer] Done producing")

async def consumer(queue, consumer_id, stop_event):
    """Consume items"""
    while not stop_event.is_set() or not queue.empty():
        try:
            item = await asyncio.wait_for(queue.get(), timeout=1.0)
            print(f"[Consumer {consumer_id}] Processing {item}")
            await asyncio.sleep(random.uniform(0.2, 0.5))
            queue.task_done()
            print(f"[Consumer {consumer_id}] Finished {item}")
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            continue

    print(f"[Consumer {consumer_id}] Stopping")

async def main():
    queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=5)
    stop_event = asyncio.Event()

    # Start consumers
    consumers = [
        asyncio.create_task(consumer(queue, i, stop_event))
        for i in range(3)
    ]

    # Produce items
    await producer(queue, 10)

    # Wait for queue to be processed
    await queue.join()

    # Stop consumers
    stop_event.set()
    await asyncio.gather(*consumers)

    print("All done!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Example 2: Priority Queue

```python
import asyncio
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any

@dataclass(order=True)
class PrioritizedItem:
    priority: int
    item: Any = field(compare=False)

async def main():
    queue = asyncio.PriorityQueue()

    # Add items with different priorities (lower = higher priority)
    items = [
        PrioritizedItem(3, "Low priority task"),
        PrioritizedItem(1, "High priority task"),
        PrioritizedItem(2, "Medium priority task"),
        PrioritizedItem(1, "Another high priority task"),
    ]

    for item in items:
        await queue.put(item)
        print(f"Added: priority={item.priority}, {item.item}")

    print("\nProcessing in priority order:")
    while not queue.empty():
        item = await queue.get()
        print(f"Got: priority={item.priority}, {item.item}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

diagrams.explain: The async version of producer–consumer: `put` suspends when the queue is full (backpressure) and `get` suspends when it is empty. Start N worker tasks, `await q.join()` to wait until every item is processed, then cancel the workers.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Gotchas
sections.body:
### Never Use threading.Lock with asyncio

```python
import asyncio
import threading

# ❌ WRONG - threading.Lock blocks the entire event loop!
thread_lock = threading.Lock()

async def bad_task():
    with thread_lock:  # BLOCKS event loop!
        await asyncio.sleep(1)

# ✅ CORRECT - asyncio.Lock yields to event loop
async_lock = asyncio.Lock()

async def good_task():
    async with async_lock:  # Yields control
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
```

### Always Use `async with` for Locks

```python
import asyncio

lock = asyncio.Lock()

# ❌ Manual acquire/release is error-prone
async def risky():
    await lock.acquire()
    try:
        await do_something()
    finally:
        lock.release()

# ✅ Context manager is safer
async def safe():
    async with lock:
        await do_something()
```
